newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Japan says future Bangladesh aid to be selective.
newsitem.headline: Japan says future Bangladesh aid to be selective.

text.p: A Japanese aid official said on Friday his country would continue giving development credit to Bangladesh, but warned that Tokyo was becoming choosy.

"We are insisting on the quality of the projects. Because the projects are with loans and the loans are to be repaid," Futao Motai, senior assistant of the Economic Cooperation Bureau of Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told a new conference in Dhaka.

"Bangladesh has, however, been repaying our loans, and (will) continue to get our assistance as long as it can afford to repay," Motai said at the end of two days of consultations with government officials on fresh Japanese soft loans.
He said he had received 10 project proposals from the Bangladesh government for funding in the energy, road, bridge, irrigation and port development sectors.
"Most of the new project proposals look fine. But we will examine those thoroughly back home and then convey our response to the Bangladesh officials," Motai said.
He declined to say what amount of fresh loans Bangladesh had sought, but finance ministry officials had earlier said Dhaka was asking for between $600 million and $700 million.
"It's not the amount we are interested in. We are looking at their merits," the Japanese official said.
Japan has been one of Bangladesh's largest donors, offering an average of $200 million worth of mostly soft loans annually.
Tokyo has denied Dhaka fresh aid pledges for the past two years, having expressed dissatisfaction at the slow pace of utilisation during the political turmoil that led to fresh elections in June.
The just-ended consultation signalled an end to the temporary freeze, officials said.

"The new government of Sheikh Hasina seems (to be) a very strong government. Their economic policies look realistic. It will be our pleasure to help the government's endeavour for economic development," Motai said.

Local newspapers on Wednesday quoted government officials as saying that Japan had warned Dhaka there could be a gradual decline in Japanese aid because of "persisting recession and rising demand from other countries". Motai declined to comment.
